en: The Treatise on the Purification of the Mind (Cittaviśuddhiprakaraṇa): [It is] without beginning or end, peaceful, devoid of existence and non-existence, free from conceptual construction, without objective support, non-abiding, and non-dual. (Cvp 1)
Without example, beyond description, inconceivable, and without demonstration;
without support, without foundation, unchanging, and unconditioned.
I take refuge in the Buddha, the support of all, whose body consists of compassion,
who reveals various skillful means for the sake of sentient beings with diverse inclinations.
Having paid homage to the Great Passion, the Lord Padmanarteśvara,
I shall here briefly speak from the perspective of self-reflection upon one's own mind.
For one who follows the method of the Yogācāra, everything is thoroughly ascertained;
all of that must be stated here, and therefore one should act accordingly.
For by whatever fierce karma sentient beings are bound,
by that very same means, through skillful method, they are liberated from the bondage of existence.
Only from the purity of a sentient being does a pure fruit arise;
this has been very clearly and extensively explained in the Mahāyāna. (Cvp 7)
The Sage proclaimed the selflessness of phenomena and persons, and that the world is mind-only;
from that [teaching], everything has arisen in accordance with the scriptures.
Urged on by compassion, he has also clearly set forth in detail, even in the scriptures, the means for those seized by the possession of the demon of grasping at existence.
All phenomena are preceded by the mind, have the mind as their chief, and are swift as the mind;
for with a serene mind one speaks or acts.
If a monk urges his elderly father, "Go quickly," and the father dies from falling as a result, he is not guilty of an immediate transgression (ānantarya).
If one who is ill causes an Arhat or another such person to suffer by pressing against them, that monk serving as an attendant incurs no fault once the patient has died. Cvp 12.

"By killing those who are not blind under the perception that they are blind, one incurs fault"—this has been clearly stated in the Vinaya; there is no fault for those whose minds are not corrupted. (Cvp 13)
There is no fault in digging up a stūpa, since it is done with the intention of restoring it;
rather, there would only be a mass of merit, because the cause for an immediate retribution has been avoided.
Having placed a pair of sandals upon the head of the sage with a virtuous intention, the two of them,
including the blind man, removed their own [suffering] and obtained the fruit of sovereignty.
Therefore, the establishment of demerit and merit is rooted in intention;
for this reason it is stated in the Āgama that there is no transgression for those with a virtuous mind.
The yogi whose self is united with his chosen deity, who exerts himself for the sake of the world,
and who enjoys sense objects, is liberated and is not defiled.
Just as one who knows the true nature of poison, upon seeing and consuming it,
merely becomes deluded and does not become free from disease.
Having observed that the entire world resembles an illusion, a mirage, a city of the Gandharvas, or a dream, what is enjoyed, by whom, how, and through what means?
The foolish are attached to forms; the mediocre attain detachment;
those of supreme intelligence, knowing the intrinsic nature of form, are liberated.

Having reflected upon the entire ritual procedure for the worship of the deity and having observed that it is pure, one should partake [of the food] without hesitation, as impelled by the mantra. (Cvp 21)
Through the union with the three syllables, one should purify, awaken, and likewise illuminate;
and with the tips of the thumb and ring finger, one should gratify the Tathāgatas.
That which is truth for the ignorant is indeed falsehood for yogins;
by this very path, going to its end, one is neither bound nor liberated.
Those who do not see reality imagine both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa;
those who do not see reality imagine neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa.
For conceptual construction is a great predator that casts one into the ocean of saṃsāra;
those of great soul who are free from conceptual construction are liberated from the bonds of existence.
Ordinary people are afflicted by the poison of doubt as if by actual venom; one whose nature is compassion should uproot that very doubt from its foundation and wander [the world].
Just as a clear crystal is colored by another dye,
so too the jewel of the mind is colored by the dye of conceptual construction.
The jewel of the mind is by its very nature secluded from conceptual constructions and passions;
it is pure from the beginning, unarisen, devoid of intrinsic nature, and untainted.
Whatever is censured by the ignorant should be performed with great effort through the yoga of one's own presiding deity, for the purpose of purifying the mind.
Deluded by the poison of the fire of passion, even those women who are objects of desire, when approached with a virtuous mind by yogins, truly bring about the fruits of both desire and liberation.
Just as one who, having meditated upon himself as Garuḍa, draws out and drinks poison,
renders the patient free from poison and is not overcome by the poison himself.
The scripture states that a wheel twelve yojanas in width was indeed revolving upon his head; having generated the thought of awakening (bodhicitta), it was removed.
Having generated the mind of awakening with a resolve set upon perfect enlightenment,
there is nothing that should not be done for the sake of the intention to rescue the world.
Seeing the world as primordially pure, unarisen, devoid of intrinsic nature, and untainted, one is neither bound nor liberated.
Having reflected according to the rule upon the extensive qualities of the deity, the yogin becomes impassioned with a mind of passion; through the enjoyment of passion, he is liberated.
What can we do? Where indeed can these various powers of existence be found?
Just as someone overcome by poison is freed from poison by means of poison itself.
The wise remove water by means of water itself, a thorn by means of a thorn itself,
and likewise passion by means of passion itself.
Just as a wise washer makes a garment free from stain by means of the stain itself,
so too should one make the self free from stain by means of the stain itself.
Just as a mirror, when thoroughly cleansed and rubbed free of dust, becomes pure, so too,
when cultivated by the wise, a fault becomes the destroyer of faults.
A lump of iron, when thrown into water, sinks indeed;
yet that very same iron, fashioned into a vessel, carries others across the blind darkness and crosses over by itself.
When the mind has been made into a vessel by means of the application of wisdom and skillful means, one who enjoys [sensual desire] is liberated; such a person liberates others as well.
Desire, when pursued by the ignorant, becomes a bond;
that very same desire, when pursued by the wise, is the means for achieving liberation.
Milk is well known throughout the entire world as the destroyer of poison;
yet that very same milk, when drunk by serpents, increases their poison all the more.
Just as the wise swan drinks the milk that has entered into water,
so too the wise man, having consumed even poisonous foods, remains liberated.
Just as even poison becomes like nectar when consumed according to the proper rules,
so too do sweetmeats such as *ghṛtapūra* become like poison for children who consume them improperly.
For this very mind, when purified by auspicious causes,
shines forth as non-conceptual, without support, and naturally stainless.
Just as this fire, though small, when refined by oil, a wick, and other such means,
becomes a lamp that is stainless, unwavering, steady, and a destroyer of darkness.
Just as a tiny banyan seed, when provided with the right conditions, brings about a great tree endowed with branches, roots, and fruit; likewise, [the seed of awakening].
Just as a different color arises from the combination of turmeric powder,
so too do they know the dharmadhātu to arise from the union of wisdom and skillful means.
Ghee mixed with honey in equal proportions becomes a poison;
yet that very same mixture, when consumed according to the prescribed rite, is a supreme elixir.
Just as copper rubbed with mercury becomes flawless gold,
so too, through the purification of knowledge, the afflictions become perfectly conducive to spiritual excellence.
For those mounted upon the Lesser Vehicle, there is fear of death at every step;
but one whose mind is set on victory in battle stands far removed from such fear.
Mounted upon the Mahāyāna, armored with the dharma of compassion,
and equipped with the needle of wisdom as his bow and arrows, he has the intention of rescuing the world.
The Great Being, possessing great skillful means, firm intellect, and free from indolence,
having conquered the difficult-to-cross battle, shall deliver others as well.
For even animals suffer, being devoted solely to their own self-interest;
blessed are those rare people who work for the benefit of the world.
Those who are greedy for their own self-interest endure sufferings such as cold and wind;
how then could those who are engaged in the welfare of the world not endure them?
Even the sufferings of the hell-beings must be endured by the compassionate;
who then would even consider the sufferings of cold winds and the like?
One should not engage in painful mental constructions, nor perform rituals through fasting;
one should avoid bathing and purification here, and abandon the customs of the village.
The nails, teeth, bones, and marrow are derived from the transformation of the father’s semen;
the flesh, blood, hair, and so forth originate from the mother’s blood.
How can such a body— a mass produced from impurity and filled with impurity—
be purified by bathing in the Gaṅgā?
For just as an impure jar does not become pure even if it is washed again and again with water,
so too this physical body, being filled with impurity, is never purified.
Just as even by bathing in the Ganges a dog does not attain purity,
so too for men who regard sacred sites with such a mindset, bathing at a tīrtha is fruitless.
If dharma were to result from bathing, then fishermen would have their purpose fulfilled;
but what need is there to mention fish and other creatures that dwell in the water day and night?
It is certain that even the destruction of evil does not occur through bathing,
since an increase in passion and other afflictions is observed among those who frequent sacred fords.
Lust, hatred, delusion, envy, and craving are always declared to be the root of evils; they cannot be purified by bathing.
These [afflictions] arise here for those born into this world due to the grasping at a self and what belongs to a self;
that [grasping], in turn, has ignorance as its cause, and that ignorance is held to be delusion.
Just as the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell ceases once the shell is seen,
so too that [cognition of a self] perishes root and branch through the vision of selflessness.
Just as the cognition of a snake regarding a rope ceases once the rope is seen,
so too the cognition of a snake will never arise there again in this life.
In this case as well, the notion of a sentient being ceases through vajra-wisdom;
no entity can arise there, just as a sprout cannot emerge from a burnt seed.
This mass, which is by nature stainless, arises from the attachment to selflessness and impurity;
that it is tormented by suffering is a misconception imagined by the foolish.
The calculation of lunar days (tithi) is also made in dependence upon the rising and setting of the moon;
likewise, the determination of day and night is established by the rising and setting of the sun.
Even the conventional usage of "east" and so forth is established in dependence upon conceptual construction;
the planets, constellations, zodiac signs, and so on, are all imagined by the entire world.
The conception of seasons, characterized by cold, heat, and rain, is likewise [mere appearance];
this experience of the fruits of one's own karma arises from the influence of auspicious and inauspicious planets.
What wise man, having set out to cleanse the wish-fulfilling gem of the mind that has been smeared with the mire of ignorance, would ever nourish that ignorance again?
There is no need for consideration of planets, lunar days, constellations, place, time, and so forth;
one should wander without conceptual construction, without signs, and free from doubt.
Whatever sense faculty comes within the range [of perception],
one should declare all of that, by its very nature, to be composed of the Buddha through the yoga of perfect meditative concentration.
The eye is the Buddha Vairocana; the ear is Vajrasūryaka;
the nose is Paramāśva; and the mouth is Padmanarteśvara.
The body is King Śrī Heruka, and the mind is Vajrasattva;
thus, the yogin, whose nature is compassion, should always conduct himself correctly in this manner.

The proponent of the final view [states]: "This one is free from conceptual construction, yet he is like one who is stable; possessing the wealth of wisdom, his activities proceed according to his will, and thus he is the enjoyer of all and the doer of all."
Performing all desired actions and acting according to his pleasure—
whether standing, sitting, walking, or likewise sleeping— Cvp_80.
Whether one has not entered a maṇḍala or is burdened by all manner of obscurations,
even one of meager merit attains accomplishment if they are devoted to the yoga of their own tutelary deity.
By this, the knower of reality attains either the state of a universal sovereign or indeed the state of a Buddha in this very life; of this there is no doubt.
Just as the world of yogins is not sublated by the ordinary world,
even yogins are sublated by those who possess progressively higher degrees of wisdom.
Through great wisdom, great skillful means, great compassion, and resolute conviction,
the Mahāyāna is taught as the sphere of activity for the Great Being.
That which was not attained even in many incalculable eons, Buddhahood itself is reached in this very birth; of this there is no doubt.
The greatness of the Mahāyāna, accumulated through merit and wisdom,
results in the attainment of the delightful state of omniscience in this very life.
However, the study of scripture, oral tradition, and reflection is not accepted in the Mahāyāna;
rather, the non-differentiation of the vehicles is proclaimed because there is no difference in their underlying intention or latent tendencies.
This resolve is indeed distinct, and likewise distinct is the conduct of awakening;
distinct also is the purification of the mind, and its fruit is described here as being blind and so forth.
Just as a form appears very clearly in a nearby stainless mirror to one with clear vision, being pure by virtue of its own transparent nature.
And likewise, the knowledge of yogins whose pure minds are free from the net of conceptual construction is like a stainless mirror of wisdom.
Just as fire suddenly blazes forth from a sun-crystal when it is touched by the rays of the sun, so too is he capable of accomplishing his own purpose.
The mind of yogis, having cast off the web of conceptual construction and resembling a sun-crystal,
blazes like that very [fire] when it is embraced by the rays of the sun of wisdom.
Just as fire blazes forth from the friction of two pieces of wood—
pure in its beginning, middle, and end, and illuminating all things—
so too do the wise know the gnosis of the yogi to arise from the union of wisdom and skillful means.
Just as this single lamp, resting upon another wick,
produces a brilliant illumination according to its own purpose and its location.
Possessing an infinite form through the meditative cultivation of wisdom and skillful means,
one should act according to the requirements of sentient beings who have various inclinations.
For just as one who knows the proper method might extract nectar from milk—
flawless, cooling, pleasing to the heart, and the destroyer of all diseases— so too [is this].
Arisen from the ritual churning of the milk of wisdom with the great skillful means,
he is the pure realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the destroyer of both pleasure and pain.
Just as a creeper that has grown forth is endowed with both flowers and fruit,
so too is the awakening in a single moment (ekakṣaṇasambodhi) joined with the two accumulations.
Whether performing subjugation, inciting hatred, immobilization, raining down, or summoning,
the yogi who delights in liquor and meat is not defiled by such acts.
Why is a mirror examined for the reflection of a hand-ornament,
since even today the power of mantras is seen within the Mahāyāna?
"In reality, no connection between mother and daughter is to be imagined here; the Tathāgata has declared that the world is like a wick of burnt iron. (Cvp 101)
Semen consists of the five elements, and blood is likewise; this body is indeed composed of them—what then is a Brahmin, and who is an outcaste?
"O monks, the body indeed consists of the five aggregates;
it is impermanent, suffering, and empty; there is neither birth nor one who is born."
Someone born from the womb of a fisherwoman, belonging to the outcaste (caṇḍāla) class, became a Brāhmaṇa through asceticism; therefore, birth is not the cause [of one's status].

A sister, a mother, a mother-in-law, one's own daughter, a niece, a Brahmin woman, a Kshatriya woman, a Vaishya woman, and even a Shudra woman— [one may approach these] through the knowledge of the ritual injunctions.
One should always honor a woman— even one who is deficient in a limb, low-born, despised, or of the lowest caste— by means of the cultivation of the vajra of knowledge.
Always with a smiling face and eyes expanded by the mantra,
one should generate the mind set on perfect enlightenment through the state of one's own chosen deity.
One should look at the visible for only a moment, and likewise hear what is to be heard;
one should speak words free from truth and falsehood, remaining unwearied.
Then, through the yoga of one's own presiding deity, one should contemplate the procedure for worship, beginning with bathing, anointing, clothing, and so forth, as well as food and drink.
One who observes the vow should engage in song, instrumental music, and likewise dance by means of the skillful method,
while refraining from any attachment to all worldly phenomena in this life.
One should not cause distress by abandoning one's own state of being through asceticism;
rather, as the Fully Awakened One did in the past, one should meditate on happiness so that it may become happiness.
"Enjoy all objects of desire through liberation from fear;
do not be afraid, for there is no sin for you—the covenant is difficult to transgress."
Even wood and other materials, when consecrated by mantras, attain the status of a deity;
how much more so a body endowed with consciousness! Alas, what a miserable display of delusion!
Having abandoned the egoity of being an ordinary person and remaining composed,
one should perform this ritual action according to the method of wisdom and means.
Just as a lotus born from the mud is not defiled by the impurities of the mud,
so the yogi is not defiled by the defects of conceptual construction and habitual tendencies.
Conceptual construction, resembling a reflection, is not defiled by defects of vision;
just as the moon in the water is never defiled by the water.
The jewel of the mind, smeared by the mire of beginningless habitual tendencies,
shines forth clearly when washed with the water of wisdom and skillful means.
For the wise one whose mind is steady through the yoga of one's own tutelary deity,
the sun of the mind shines forth, liberated from the clouds of wrong views.
Because the true nature of reality is determined through the discernment of the characteristics of wisdom,
the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) is to be accepted by abandoning the reversal caused by ignorance.
When the jar of conceptual construction is suddenly shattered by the hammer of wisdom,
the lamp of knowledge— naturally stainless and clear— shines forth.
The well-known elements— earth, fire, water, and air—
are indeed transformed otherwise by those who lack true knowledge through the application of the power of mantras.
Having abandoned all other doctrines, one should practice the doctrine of mantra;
for by the power of that mantra, even the state of bliss is accomplished.
One must not abandon the Three Jewels, nor the thought of awakening, nor one’s guru. No living beings whatsoever are to be killed, and one should also uphold the commitments.
Honey, blood, camphor, combined with red sandalwood,
and the water of the sage-vajra— one should consecrate these five as well.
With other divine methods that cause the elevation of the mind,
one should gratify the Mind-Vajra in order to pacify the agitation of the vital winds.
One should not suspect impurity; endowed with the play of non-conceptual yoga, the practitioner of mantra should perform everything with a mind thus united.
One is overcome even by poison the size of a fly's foot;
yet a minute amount of aversion is joined with the hardship of fear of death.
A wise man should either engage in a fair fight or flee well;
for an intermediate state is futile, as it will surely result in a downfall.
One should not transgress the command of the guru, nor his seal, nor even his shadow;
one should always accept his virtues, and never his faults.
The teacher is the supreme deity; he should be worshipped with great effort.
He is the King who himself dwells in visible form as the Holder of the Vajra.
Just as a pure water-jewel purifies turbid water,
so too is the jewel of faith said to purify the jewel of the mind.
Even one who possesses faith may become deluded if he is devoid of the eye of wisdom;
therefore, one should generate wisdom, which consists of both scriptural tradition and realization.
Faithful, learned, wise, and by nature compassionate,
he finds the means for happiness in order to destroy the suffering of the world.
Whatever happiness has been acquired by me through maintaining purity of mind,
may all people become happy by means of that same maintenance of purity of mind.
"This is the work of the venerable Āryadeva."
